reason: The sources provide rich, verified details across independent sites detailing M87's discovery, relativistic jet, supermassive black hole, and imaging history.
story: In 1781, Charles Messier spotted a strange smudge in Virgo, cataloging it as nebula M87. Over a century later in 1918, astronomer Heber Curtis looked through the Lick Observatory telescope and noticed something bizarre: a thin, straight ray shooting out of the object's core. That ray was an energetic plasma jet stretching roughly 5,000 light-years into deep space, powered by a central cosmic engine. When the Hubble Space Telescope and later ground arrays zoomed in, they discovered a gargantuan rotating accretion disk feeding a supermassive black hole with billions of times the mass of the Sun. Traveling at relativistic speeds, knots in the jet even appear to move faster than light due to an optical illusion. In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope finally captured the historic first direct picture of this shadow, turning a faint 18th-century smudge into humanity's iconic gateway to black hole physics.
angle: Over a century ago in 1918, astronomers spotted a curious straight beam of light erupting from M87—humanity's first glimpse of a relativistic jet blasting 5,000 light-years from a supermassive black hole.

claims.claim: Charles Messier discovered and cataloged M87 in 1781.
M87 is an enormous elliptical galaxy located in the Virgo Cluster.
M87 is also designated as NGC 4486 and the radio source Virgo A.
M87 is situated roughly 53 to 55 million light-years away from Earth.
In 1918, Heber Curtis of Lick Observatory discovered a straight ray of matter emerging from M87's center.
The plasma jet extends roughly 5,000 light-years from the galactic nucleus.
Light from the jet is strongly polarized, characteristic of synchrotron radiation produced in magnetic fields.
Gas clouds in M87's jet exhibit apparent superluminal motion, an optical illusion caused by the jet traveling near the speed of light toward the observer.
Innokentii Balanowski discovered a magnitude 11.5 supernova on 1919 photographic plates of M87 in 1922.
M87 hosts a vast population of several thousand to roughly 15,000 globular clusters, far outnumbering the Milky Way's 150 to 200.
Post-repair Hubble Space Telescope observations identified a rotating gaseous accretion disk surrounding a central mass of 2 to 3 billion solar masses.
The Event Horizon Telescope collected observational data in 2017 to produce the first-ever direct image of M87's supermassive black hole, unveiled in 2019.
The central black hole M87* has a mass calculated at approximately 6.5 billion times the mass of the Sun.
The Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration released an updated image of M87* in polarized light revealing the structure of surrounding magnetic fields.
In 2023, astrophysicists applied a machine learning technique called PRIMO to sharpen the original EHT image of M87*.
M87 is accompanied by satellite dwarf galaxies including NGC 4478 and NGC 4486B.

disputed: Distance and jet length: S1 cites ~53.5 million light-years and a jet length of ~4,900–5,000 light-years, while S3 and S4 cite 55 million light-years, with S4 suggesting the jet could reach 7,000 to 8,000 light-years based on revised distances. Scripts should say 'roughly 53 to 55 million light-years away' and 'at least 5,000 light-years long'.

Central black hole mass measurements: 1990s Hubble spectroscopic data estimated 2.4 billion solar masses (S1, S4), whereas 2019 EHT measurements derived 6.5 billion solar masses (S1, S3). Scripts should attribute the 6.5-billion figure specifically to the Event Horizon Telescope's horizon-scale measurements.

Central black hole offset: S1 notes a 2010 claim that M87* was physically displaced 7 parsecs from the galactic center, but subsequent 2011 and 2018 studies determined the apparent offset was caused by brightness fluctuations in the jet. Scripts should omit the offset claim or note it was debunked.
